statement: Some people say that governments should tax unhealthy foods and drinks to encourage better diets. Others feel that what people choose to eat is a matter of personal responsibility.
question: Discuss both these views and give your own opinion.
model:
As rates of obesity and diabetes climb in many countries, governments have begun to consider whether taxes on sugary drinks and processed snacks could steer people towards healthier diets. Some see such measures as sensible public policy, while others regard them as unwarranted interference. On balance, I believe that carefully designed food taxes are justified.

Those who oppose these taxes argue that adults should be free to decide what they eat, even if their choices are unwise. In their view, the state has no business penalising someone for enjoying a fizzy drink or a chocolate bar, and doing so treats citizens like children. There is also a fairness objection: because poorer households spend a larger share of their income on food, a tax on cheap, calorie-dense products falls hardest on those who can least afford it.

Advocates, however, contend that food choices are far from entirely free. Manufacturers spend enormous sums designing products that are as tempting as possible and marketing them relentlessly, often to children. Moreover, the consequences of poor diet are not purely personal, since treating diet-related illnesses places a heavy burden on public health services funded by every taxpayer. The evidence also suggests that such taxes work. When Britain introduced a levy on sugary soft drinks in 2018, many manufacturers quietly reduced the sugar content of their products to avoid it, so consumers benefited without necessarily paying more.

Personally, I find the second argument more persuasive, provided that the policy addresses its weaknesses. Revenue raised from food taxes should be spent on subsidising fruit and vegetables or funding healthy school meals, which would offset the burden on low-income families.

In conclusion, although personal responsibility matters, individuals make choices within an environment shaped by powerful commercial interests. Well-designed taxes help to rebalance that environment and protect public health.
